mcq.QUESTION_DESC: What is the primary performance metric for pipelined processors?
What is the formula for pipeline throughput?
Which register tracks instructions across pipeline stages?
How do data hazards affect pipeline performance?
What is the impact of a branch misprediction on performance?

sq.ANSWER: 1. Pipelining is a technique used in computer architecture to improve instruction throughput. It divides the instruction execution process into several stages, with each stage handling a part of the instruction, such as fetch, decode, execute, memory access, and write-back. Multiple instructions are overlapped in execution by processing different stages simultaneously, similar to an assembly line in manufacturing. This increases CPU efficiency by executing more instructions per unit time, even though the time to complete a single instruction remains the same.

1. Pipeline performance can be affected by several factors:

  2. Pipeline hazards: Data hazards (dependency between instructions), control hazards (branch instructions), and structural hazards (resource conflicts) can cause pipeline stalls.

  3. Pipeline stalls or bubbles: Introduced to resolve hazards, these reduce throughput.

  4. Branch penalties: Incorrect branch predictions force the pipeline to discard fetched instructions.

  5. Pipeline depth: Deeper pipelines increase throughput but can suffer more from hazards.
    Effective hazard detection and resolution techniques are necessary to maintain pipeline efficiency.
sq.QUESTION_DESC: Describe the factors that can affect the performance of a pipeline.

lq.ANSWER:
Speedup due to pipelining is the ratio of the execution time of non-pipelined processor to the execution time of a pipelined processor.

Ideal Speedup Calculation:

  • If the processor has k pipeline stages, and each instruction takes k cycles in a non-pipelined processor, then the execution time for n instructions is:
    Tnon−pipelined=n×k×tT_{non-pipelined} = n \times k \times tTnon−pipelined​=n×k×t where ttt is the clock cycle time.

  • In an ideal pipelined processor, the pipeline is filled and one instruction completes every cycle after the initial fill:
    Tpipelined=(k+n−1)×tpT_{pipelined} = (k + n - 1) \times t_pTpipelined​=(k+n−1)×tp​, where tpt_ptp​ is the pipeline clock cycle time.

  • Assuming tp≈tkt_p \approx \frac{t}{k}tp​≈kt​, the ideal speedup is:

    Speedup=n×k×t(k+n−1)×tk=n×k2k+n−1\text{Speedup} = \frac{n \times k \times t}{(k + n -1) \times \frac{t}{k}} = \frac{n \times k^2}{k + n - 1}Speedup=(k+n−1)×kt​n×k×t​=k+n−1n×k2​

  • For large nnn, speedup approaches kkk (number of stages).

Factors Affecting Actual Speedup:

  1. Pipeline Hazards:

    • Structural hazards: Resource conflicts reduce pipeline efficiency.

    • Data hazards: Instruction dependencies may cause stalls.

    • Control hazards: Branch instructions can cause pipeline flushing.

  2. Pipeline Fill and Drain Time:

    • Initial latency for pipeline to fill and drain at the end.

  3. Unequal Stage Delays:

    • The slowest stage dictates the clock cycle time, reducing speedup.

  4. Overheads from Control and Forwarding:

    • Additional logic to handle hazards can slow down clock or cause bubbles.

Conclusion:
Ideal speedup is approximately equal to the number of pipeline stages, but actual speedup is reduced by hazards, stalls, and implementation overheads.
